newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy markets face uncertainty on French left win.
newsitem.headline: Italy markets face uncertainty on French left win.

text.p: Italian financial markets face a period of increased uncertainty as a Socialist victory in French elections heightens worries that Europe's single currency may be undermined at its birth, analysts said on Monday.

Although the French left is committed to Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), it does not support austerity measures of the previous government and a watering down of the Maastricht Treaty criteria now seems likely, the economists said.

The French Socialists want a broad EMU at its start to include Italy, Spain and Portugal rather than a narrow EMU leaving out the three Mediterranean countries, but this could mean softer entry terms and an increased risk of a delay.
"The most likely scenario is a broad EMU on softer terms," said Alex Garrard, international economist at UBS in London.

He added that the EMU debate had now shifted from uncertainty over whether it would include a narrow or broad group of nations, and had polarised towards a debate over softer terms for EMU and a possible delay in the start-up date.

"The market looks at reality not political will and in reality softer Maastricht requirements will mean a weaker euro and higher interest rate levels in Europe," said Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest in Milan.
Italian financial markets slipped lower in Monday trading but then steadied, as dealers pondered what a watered down single currency would mean for investing in Italian assets.
At 1205 GMT, the June BTP bond future on London's LIFFE market firmed 26 basis points to 129.16 after an early low of 128.23, with a yield spread over German bunds at 135 bps.
Many analysts have been forecasting the spread to widen out to 150, representing a greater risk premium attached to investing in Italian bonds.

Milan stocks eased then recovered, while the lira showed a firmer trend after Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio appeared to show some reluctance to ease monetary policy in a speech to the Bank of Italy's annual assembly on Saturday.
NatWest's De Gregorio points out that although the lira may benefit from a stronger dollar, it will suffer as it is perceived in a new Euro as the "weak wagon in a weak train".

Italy has made great strides to get its finances in order to enter EMU in the first wave, and prime minister Romano Prodi has committed his government to enter EMU at its scheduled start at the beginning of 1999.

By putting the lira in a strong EMU centred on a strong German mark, Italy had hoped to show financial markets a determined front in keeping its finances in order. This scenario seems less and less likely, economists said.

They noted Italy has already pushed through unprecedent fiscal tightening and has one of the highest real interest rates in the western world. This has helped push Italy into a technical recession of two successive quarters of negative growth in the last quarter of 1996 and the first of 1997.
They point out that with two major players on the brink of political crisis the problems of EMU are growing by the day.

The German government is embroiled in a row with the Bundesbank opposed to the Bonn plan to revalue its gold reserves to reach the Maastricht criteria, while a new left French government faces "cohabiting" with conservative President Jacques Chirac.
